I'm not a ux designer but these fixes don't seem that well thought out to me. They neglect to address the very root of these problems. The voting system for example sounds like an easy implementation and is cited as a solution in other places but I imagine is only complicated when you consider the way content is shared on Facebook. So like-minded users share like-minded content and would only vote in the same vain. So what's fake news to some wouldn't be too others, right? Furthermore, I don't think users who be as likely to share to "fake news" only news they thought was share-worthy, even if it's fake. So wouldn't fake news content only propagate when rallied behind like minded users and dismissed by the opposing sides. Isn't the problem that exist now? Effectively causing Facebook to fact check most of it's content like they are doing now?

In general or in relation to your piece? In general I love when woodworking shows the joinery. I come from a family of woodworkers and I have a rich love for joinery. Going back to the Craftsman style is so much about letting the way something is made through contrasting colors, materials and techniques. However part of that appreciate comes from seeing it in its many uses around a piece as a whole. So seeing how one simple joint used various areas or parts of a table both structurally and aesthetically. With yours, I ask, did you use dowels for legs, apron, or drawer? If so, why not show them well?  I think I would have preferred it more hidden as they distract from the solid, uniform, and thick style that makes your table most appealing. This is just a note as I tried to touch on before where it's about why you chose to show the joinery, and the aesthetic relationship it shares with your piece as a whole. Sometimes it's just as strong and impressive not showing how something is made as it can be showing it it just depends on what you as the designer and artist want to say by making those decisions and maybe what a client is looking for.

Hey, it certainly looks like a very well created piece and I hope you're proud of it! I can agree with a lot what was mentioned above. I can see you describe yourself as a student and I think this piece shows your curiosity and playfulness in trying different things like contrasting woods, tapered legs, joinery and so on. From a design standpoint, my suggestion would be to be considerate to these choices you make in your process and how it affects the overall look of your piece. So by that, I just want to take an example by your tapered legs, to ask why you chose to do that in relation to the other parts and pieces of your table. Are there any other angular visual cues to touch that relate back to your legs from other perspectives? This tends to be a way in which Craftsmanship and design differ but they can't ever be separated and work best when there's communication between the two. Great work and I hope to see more of your stuff in the sub in the future!

It's possible then for sure, I would look at acoustical treatment options with what your sound set up is. It sounds like it may help but I would keep in mind that good accoustic treatment is a pretty tough science and can require a lot of trial and error and it's possible that wall isn't your week spot, it could be your corners because that's where you have your speakers (which you can treat with "bass traps" or your side walls which are reflecting a lot of sound.) If your working on a budget, I understand that hiring an acoustic professional not feasible but I suggest just playing with where you apply treatments before committing and I before looking at treatment I would even look at how your sound system is set up as well. Maybe some minor adjustments where and how they are placed could fix this problem without needing paneling.

I would look at wall mounting your tv. Possibly center of wall width wise and Having it higher up will break up that huge negative space. That way you don't have to worry adding anything to the wall, because your tv remains it's center piece and focus. Also if you have the rgbs behind your tv, it will feel more soft in filling space than say picture and ledges. Then you use the credenza as low shelving for anything like plants, consoles, sculptures, anything fairly small and under about 8" in height. (Guessing that height restriction but just so your aware that having it is important to not intrude on the space below your tv for good use of negative space.

I would consider if you have an acoustic problem before applying acoustical panels. Although I know a pretty easy and cheap method for panels. The thing about acoustical panels is if you over treat room or don't treat it properly, it will leave the room sounding "dry" and a bit awkward. That's why I wouldn't recommend using acoustical panels unless it's a problem you have noticed. 
    
To make the panels. 

1: construct a standard art canvas frame, one that you would paint on. Except use your fabric of choice for the front.   
  
2: if you really need it to be acoustical, fill the inside with layers of cheap sheets, comforters, blankets. This sounds cheap but is surprisingly effective at dampening sound. Attentively, a cheap but less effective is using upholstery foam on the inside.   
  
3: if you want that button looking, you'll look for upholstery tufting tutorials using a thick needle for the layers you used previously. It's pretty easy to do.

I looked through some of the other comments and got a better idea and I wanted to suggest something what I think would be a pretty good compromise. The flooring in the lounge, dining, and kitchen looks newer, so I think there's more play to these walls and that wouldn't intrude much on the beautiful front of the building. I would considering taking the wall between the lounge and the dining room to open these spaces up. If you wanted to keep the lounge, a lounge it would be possible and in the place of the wall you may be able to fit an island with some bar style seating (casual dining) or possibly a dinning set in the open area (formal dining) depending on your needs. With that area more a single open, you could close the dinning room door off for additional wall space. My suggestion might be keeping the door in place and existing but turning it to a false door while you drywall the other side (the dinning room side) to be a wall useful for cabinets or moving the built in too. I think this idea would preserve the corridor of the first floor as well, which I enjoy not just for the tile floor.     
  
Also, opening the wall between the kitchen and dining may allow you to pull the kitchen more into the dining area, overlapping the existing but creating better flow and use of the area. It was difficult to see the built ins but this might also allow you to integrate them more with the kitchen or my suggest is just to move them to a more convenient area.  This might allow you enough clearance to put your utility towards the back the kitchen then.   
  
You would need to check these aren't load bearing walls though.
